# SERVICE THAT FITS THE MARKET
## A regional operating framework for customer service, satisfaction and loyalty
**Proposal for regional leadership and the Global Service Council | v1.0**

**Decision sought:** adoption of (a) the four-layer service structure and decision rights, (b) the contact-intent taxonomy as the design unit, (c) the twelve intervention tracks, and (d) funding for the Diagnostic Gate. **All quantities are design targets calibrated at the Diagnostic Gate and returned for approval before anything is promised to customers.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to improve "customer service" and start eliminating the reasons customers have to contact us.** Regional satisfaction problems are almost never solved by adding headcount, extending hours or bolting on a chatbot; they are solved by separating three fundamentally different things that our current operation blends into one queue: **failure demand** (contacts caused by our own defects — wrong ETAs, opaque returns, failed payments), **value demand** (contacts where the customer legitimately needs help or advice), and **relationship moments** (contacts where the customer's trust is either won or destroyed). Each requires a different design. Therefore: adopt a **four-layer model** — a thin, non-waivable **Service Spine** (seven promises that make us one brand); a **Regional Dial** set by [Market M] against a published dossier of language, channel, payment, logistics and regulatory realities; a **Journey Charter** per contact-intent family, owned by a named cross-functional owner with authority over the upstream defect, not just the queue; and a **Frontline Authority** layer that gives the person actually talking to the customer a published, funded right to resolve. Work the twelve tracks in §5 in sequence — **failure demand first, because it is the cheapest satisfaction gain we will ever buy** — and measure with a metric triad (§8) that makes it impossible to hide a bad experience behind a good average. **One constraint governs everything: the Resolution Rule (§3) — every contact is resolved at the earliest point that can see the customer's whole problem, and no later.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every percentage, hour, currency value, SLA and threshold below is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use. They exist because a proposal with no numbers cannot be argued with. **The Diagnostic Gate (§9) replaces them with measured values**; leadership approves the calibrated set before any customer-facing commitment is made.

Market-specific variables — language(s) and dialects, dominant messaging platform, payment mix, address conventions, delivery-partner mix, consumer-protection law, cultural norms around complaint and confrontation — are deliberately left as **[Market M variables]** and filled at the Diagnostic Gate. A framework that pretends to know these in advance is the first cause of the problem we are trying to fix.

### 0.2 Who this covers

"Customer service" is routinely used as a synonym for "the contact centre." That framing guarantees failure, because most of what determines satisfaction happens before anyone contacts us and is owned by teams who never see a ticket.

| Population | Illustrative share of contact volume *[target]* | What "better service" means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Self-resolvers** | ~[55]% | Never needing us; and when they do, resolving it themselves *in seconds, inside the app* | §5 Tracks 1–4 |
| **B. Assisted resolvers** | ~[35]% | Reaching a competent human fast, once, in their language, with authority to fix it | §5 Tracks 5–8 |
| **C. High-stakes / high-emotion** | ~[10]% | Being *held* — ownership, proactive updates, real remedy, follow-up | §5 Tracks 9–12 |
| **D. Silent dissatisfied** | Invisible in ticket data; possibly [2–4]× population C | Being *detected* without contacting us at all | §8.3 |

**Rule of the document:** population D is the one that churns. Any metric set that cannot see it is a vanity metric. Every reporting cut in §8 includes a silent-signal panel.

Also in scope, and usually omitted: **the frontline agents themselves** (§6). Agent experience is not a welfare topic; it is the single largest controllable input to customer satisfaction, and in this market it is currently a bottleneck.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The regional feedback says "support is not meeting expectations." That sentence contains no diagnosis. Reframe it:

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we improve our support channels? | Why are customers contacting us at all, and which contacts are our own defects? |
| How do we reduce response time? | How do we reduce *time to resolution* — and how often do we make the customer come back a second time? |
| Should we add a chatbot? | Which contacts have low consequence and high machine confidence — and which must never touch automation? |
| Are customers satisfied? | Are they *returning*, buying across categories, and telling us the truth — and which segments have gone quiet? |
| What's our CSAT? | What is our CSAT **for the journeys we handle worst**, in the local language, at the local peak? |
| Why is this market underperforming? | Which of our global defaults are simply wrong here — channel, language, payment, returns, tone, hours? |

**Corollary 1 — Contact volume is a defect signal, not a workload forecast.** The default operational reflex is to staff to demand. The correct first reflex is to ask which demand should not exist. Every recurring contact reason is an unpaid invoice from another department.

**Corollary 2 — Most regional dissatisfaction is not a service problem.** It is a **promise problem** (ETAs we cannot keep), a **legibility problem** (policies written for a different market), a **language problem** (translated, not localised), a **channel problem** (we offer email; they live on messaging), or an **authority problem** (agents who must escalate to help). Fixing these is cheaper than expanding the centre, and it compounds. **Sequence them first.**

**Corollary 3 — Satisfaction and loyalty are not the same objective.** Satisfaction is the absence of friction. Loyalty is the presence of reciprocity — a memory of being treated well when it would have been easy to treat us badly. A programme that only removes friction produces indifferent customers who leave for a discount. Tracks 9–12 exist for this reason.

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

**A gate, not a priority — Regulatory, data and consumer-protection integrity.** No arrangement that breaches [Market M] consumer law (return windows, refund timelines, warranty duties, cooling-off rights), data-residency or privacy rules, marketing-consent rules, accessibility obligations, or any outsourcing/labour agreement covering frontline staff. Applied as pass/fail *before* options are compared. Legal and DPO hold a veto, not an opinion. Automated decisioning that affects a customer's money is in scope of this gate.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Trust** | Customers believe our promises (ETA accuracy, refund actually arriving on the day stated) and believe we will make things right |
| **2** | **Effective resolution** | The customer's problem is *gone*, first time, without a second contact |
| **3** | **Effortlessness** | Time and steps the customer spends, measured in *their* terms, not ours |
| **4** | **Relationship depth** | Repeat purchase, category expansion, willingness to be contacted, advocacy |
| **5** | **Cost to serve** | Fully-loaded cost per resolved contact, and per *retained* customer |

Trust outranks resolution because a fast fix inside a system that lies about delivery dates buys nothing. Cost is last because savings taken out of trust are borrowed, not earned — and in this market, evidently, already overdrawn.

### 2.1 Adjudication

- Conflicts are decided by the **Regional Service Council** (§7.1) on a written submission naming the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the customer population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A containment or automation proposal that reduces trust must quantify both the saving and the harm and propose mitigation. "It deflects [X]% of contacts" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **Regional MD + Global Service Head** sign-off and entry in the Exception Register with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions. Precedent is how a federated service model stays coherent without a 400-page script library.

---

## §3 The Resolution Rule and the four layers

> **Resolution Rule:** Every customer problem is resolved at the earliest point that can see the whole problem — and no later. Every *policy* about resolution is set at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects — and no lower.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Service Spine** | Global Service Council | 7 promises. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual |
| **Regional Dial** | [Market M] leadership + CX + Legal + Logistics | Channel mix, languages and dialects, hours, remedy menu and values, returns/refund mechanics, payment-failure handling, tone-of-voice guide, escalation ladder, partner SLAs | Quarterly |
| **Journey Charter** | Named cross-functional Journey Owner per contact-intent family (§4) | Root-cause backlog, self-service flow, automation boundary, agent playbook, target metrics, defect SLA on upstream teams | Monthly review, published |
| **Frontline Authority** | Agent, within published guardrails | Resolve, refund, replace, waive, expedite, gift — up to a funded discretion limit, without escalation | Continuous; audited monthly |

### 3.1 The Service Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**P1 — We tell the truth about time.** Every promise we display (delivery, refund, response, repair) is a commitment we measure ourselves against publicly, with an honest confidence range rather than an optimistic point estimate. Under-promise; over-deliver.

**P2 — One contact, one owner.** A customer never re-explains their problem. Ownership transfers with full context; the customer is never the integration layer between our departments.

**P3 — Never a dead end.** Every automated interaction has a visible, one-tap route to a human. Automation may triage, draft, translate and act; it may not trap.

**P4 — The frontline can fix things.** Every agent has published authority to resolve up to a defined value without permission. Escalation is a design failure, tracked as such.

**P5 — Local by default, not translated.** Language, tone, channel, examples, payment methods, address handling and holiday calendars are set locally. Global templates are a starting point, never a requirement.

**P6 — Accessible to everyone who buys from us.** Low-bandwidth paths, voice options where literacy or connectivity demand it, screen-reader compliance, and a channel that works on the devices our customers actually own.

**P7 — Every recurring contact reason has an owner outside the contact centre.** Service reports the defect; the defect's owner is accountable for eliminating it, on a clock.

Seven is the ceiling. Anything added must be simultaneously true, legal, affordable and culturally legible in every market we operate.

---

## §4 The design unit: contact intents, not channels

Organising service by channel (phone team, email team, chat team) guarantees inconsistency, because the *same* problem gets a different answer depending on where the customer knocked. Organise instead by **intent**, and route intent to the treatment it deserves.

| # | Intent | Discriminating test | Correct treatment | Automation suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I1** | **Status anxiety** — "where is my order?" | Customer wants information we already hold | **Eliminate**: proactive push, accurate tracking, live ETA | Full — but the real answer is prevention |
| **I2** | **Transaction change** — reschedule, reroute, cancel, address fix | Customer wants a *state change*, not advice | **Self-serve action**, one tap, instant confirmation | Full, if the flow *acts* rather than explains |
| **I3** | **Something is broken** — wrong, damaged, missing, late, payment failed | A promise was broken | **Human or high-confidence auto-remedy, plus root-cause capture** | Partial; consequence is high |
| **I4** | **Advice and decision help** — sizing, fit, compatibility, comparison | Customer needs judgement to buy | **Assisted commerce** — expert humans, community, rich content | Assist only; converts revenue |
| **I5** | **Trust rupture** — anger, unfairness, repeated failure, public complaint, vulnerability | The relationship is at stake | **Named senior owner, generous fast remedy, follow-up** | **Never automate** |

**The two intents teams confuse:** I1 and I3. "Where is my order" *after* a missed promise is not I1 — it is I3 wearing I1's clothes, and answering it with a tracking link is how a recoverable failure becomes churn. Detection logic for this is a Diagnostic Gate deliverable.

**Design implication:** I1 and I2 are, we believe, the majority of current contact volume in [Market M] — *this is a hypothesis, not a finding*, and it is the Diagnostic Gate's first test. If confirmed, the highest-return investment is not the contact centre at all.

---

## §5 The twelve intervention tracks

Ordered by sequence, not by ambition. Tracks 1–4 pay for the rest.

### Wave 1 — Eliminate failure demand *(weeks 0–12)*

**Track 1 — Contact-reason forensics and defect ownership.**
Re-code the last [12] months of contacts into the I1–I5 taxonomy plus a root-cause layer (carrier, catalogue, payment, policy, UX, our own message). Publish a weekly **Top 20 Contact Reasons** board with a named owner *outside* service for each, a defect SLA *[target: root cause fixed or mitigation shipped within 60 days]*, and a visible cost-of-failure figure per reason. **Innovation is not required here; accountability is.** Expected volume reduction: *[target: 20–30% within two quarters]*.

**Track 2 — Honest promises engine.**
Replace optimistic single-date ETAs with locally calibrated, confidence-ranged promises computed per postcode/partner/product/season. Deliberately pad the customer-facing promise while optimising the internal target; measure **promise-kept rate**, not average delivery time. In markets with volatile last-mile, this single change typically moves satisfaction more than any contact-centre investment.

**Track 3 — Proactive disruption service.**
Detect the failure before the customer does — carrier exception, customs hold, weather event, stock-out, failed payment, address ambiguity — and reach out first with (a) what happened, (b) what we've already done, (c) two choices, (d) a remedy already applied where we were at fault. **The default is not "notify"; it is "notify and resolve in the same message."** Preventing an I1/I3 contact is worth several times containing one.

**Track 4 — Self-service that acts.**
Retire FAQ-as-service. Every I2 intent becomes a one-tap action in-app and in the order confirmation: reschedule, reroute, change address, cancel, return, exchange, split delivery, refund-to-original-method. Embedded contextually at the point of friction, not buried in a help centre. Target: *[80]% of I2 resolved without human contact and without customer effort exceeding [3] taps.*

### Wave 2 — Rebuild assisted service for this market *(weeks 8–24)*

**Track 5 — Channel realism.**
Meet customers where they already are. Move the primary assisted channel to **[Market M's dominant messaging platform]** with full commerce and identity integration, asynchronous by design, threaded so history persists and P2 is structurally guaranteed. Retain voice for I3/I5 and for segments that prefer it; retain a low-bandwidth path. **Do not add channels — replace them.** Channel proliferation is how consistency dies.

**Track 6 — Localisation, not translation.**
Native speakers of [Market M languages and principal dialects], locally written tone-of-voice guide (directness, formality, apology conventions, how complaint is culturally expressed), local holiday and peak calendars, local payment-failure playbooks (including cash-on-delivery, instalments, wallet mechanics as applicable), local address-normalisation logic, local returns network (partner stores, lockers, pickup points) instead of an imported courier-only model. Hire a small number of **service designers who are from this market**, not global staff on rotation.

**Track 7 — The AI/human boundary, drawn on two axes.**
Automate on **confidence × consequence**, never on cost alone.

| | Low consequence | High consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **High machine confidence** | **Automate fully** (I1, I2) | **Automate the action, notify a human owner** (auto-refund with audit) |
| **Low machine confidence** | **Automate triage; human resolves** | **Human only, senior, no bot in the path** (I5) |
